ch25.note: China's trunk railways were each named for their two end cities—here Tianjin and Pukou (the Yangtze bank opposite Nanjing); so too the Beiping–Hankou, Canton–Kowloon, Beiping–Suiyuan, and Jiao–Ji lines named nearby. As the arteries that carried Japanese troops and supplies, these were the prime targets of Juntong sabotage.

For the war the Nationalists divided the front into numbered 'war zones' (战区), each a standing regional command. The Eighth War Zone covered the northwest—Gansu, Ningxia, and part of Suiyuan—with its headquarters at Lanzhou under Zhu Shaoliang.

The English name, in the Shanghai International Settlement, for the road running past Jing'an Temple—named for a famous 'bubbling well' or spring there. 'Jing'an' is the Chinese name of the same district; the two names in the text mark one place (today's Nanjing West Road).

A powerful semi-autonomous militarist faction based in Guangxi province and led by Li Zongren and Bai Chongxi—nominally under Chiang's central government but keeping its own army and networks, and often at odds with Nanjing.

ch25.anchor: engaged as adviser by a certain department of our government
ch25.note: From 1928 the Nationalist government employed a mission of German officers—culminating with von Seeckt and von Falkenhausen—to build and train a modern army. Berlin recalled the mission in 1938 as Germany drew closer to Japan, leaving stray German advisers, like the man Chen keeps anonymous here, privately in China.

The Nine Tripods (九鼎) were the ancient bronze cauldrons, cast in legend by Yu the Great, that stood for rightful sovereignty over the realm. 'A word weighing as the nine tripods' (一言九鼎) means a promise of the utmost, binding weight.
